## The founder-emulation items

1. **Who (practitioner `agent`).** YC-C names hotel groups with "call centers and central reservation departments";
   YC-L's video features front-desk staff at a Munich hotel. *My choice:* the reservation agent, central office or
   front desk, who sees the missed-call list. Segment: hotel groups in Germany with a central office or call center.
2. **When (circumstance, occasion, window).** YC-L's "After hours. During peak hours. On holidays." *My choice:* the
   occasion "reservation shift", window the last 7 days (calls come in on every shift; spec 120's "every shift" -> 7
   DAYS), Frequency 5 to 7 days out of 7.
3. **Who pays (decision-maker `director`, Buyer and payer, Purchase friction).** TERMS addresses the hotel group;
   YC-L asks to "book a 10-minute call if you lead a hotel group". *My choice:* the revenue or reservations director
   decides, the hotel's owner has to agree. Purchase friction tests "A data protection review of guest calls" (German
   hotels handle guests' card and personal data on the call); my choice, no source names it.
4. **Mechanism.** YC-C: missed calls forwarded to Codyco, the AI answers, bookings appear in the PMS. Compatibility
   tests call forwarding (the mechanism needs it); Adoption friction tests letting the AI answer in the hotel's voice.
5. **Cost, price, ability.** As in the table. Reading `budget` by the engine (a percent of calls against euros).
6. **Commitment.** TERMS and YC-L: the paid, money-back pilot at one location. The step carries its number ("pay
   €3,000 for a money-back pilot at one hotel"), the gap-8 check.

## The respondents

No first-person account by a German reservation agent or revenue director was found in public (no HN thread; the
site's quotes are curated testimonials). **Every person is the author's invention**, no real person's name is used,
and each is built on the public facts named here.

Reservation agents (Parts 1 and 2):
- Lena Hoffmann: a trade-fair Saturday in a Munich central office; built on YC-L ("During peak hours") and the Munich
  hotel YC-L features.
- Murat Yilmaz: a check-in rush at the desk; YC-L's "peak hours".
- Chiara Russo: a group whose call center already answers after hours (YC-C: "Even with call centers..."); her pain is
  group emails, so Importance and Current solution go against the founder.
- Jonas Weber: alone on a Sunday desk; YC-L's "On holidays" / after hours.
- Aylin Demir: an old phone system that cannot forward (Compatibility only_with_help); the author's.
- Tobias Brandl: the sceptic who will not hand guests to an AI (Relative advantage negative, Adoption no); the author's.
- Elif Kaya: weekend abandoned calls seen on Monday; YC-L's "After hours".
- Daniel Okonkwo: rates pushed wrong to agencies matter more (Importance against); the author's.
- Mehmet Arslan: a vague story, GUESSED. Katarina Novak: a story chip, GUESSED.
- Florian Gruber, Nadia Haddad: gate No (no unanswered booking call in the 7 days).

Revenue directors (COMMERCIAL_B2B link, Part 3): Stefanie Wagner (6%), Andreas Keller (4%, below the founder's 5%),
Roberto Bianchi (8%), Ingrid Lindholm (2%, a call center covers after hours), Karim Benali (does not know his rate;
YC-L's "Free AI Strategy Workshop" and SITE's free test number as his ask), Petra Vogel (5%), Hannes Moser (nothing,
would not pay), Joanna Wiśniewska (10% at resort hotels in high season). The value boxes are percents of the calls, in
the founder's unit and period; the price picks are two codes, the pilot's rung and the licence's rung, each placed
against the founder's €3,000 and €1,000.

## Status today

Same idea (SITE, 2026-10-22): "Turn missed hotel calls into paid bookings.", widened to payments, invoices and
handovers; "Running at 15+ hotel groups" (the launch said 7); "€10k+ bookings written directly into the PMS". **No
public price today** (SITE and /faq show none); the €3,000 pilot terms remain the only priced source.

## Open (what could not be sourced, and the workarounds)

- **The licence amount** was never public. €1,000 to €1,500 per hotel a month is the operator's reading of the pilot's
  monthly rate (above). Treat the plan step's reading as a reading of that derivation.
- **Dollars or euros.** YC-L says "$5,000", YC-C "€5,000" for the same hotel; the pilot fee is in euros and the company
  is in Munich, so the entry is in euros. The market is DE, and the golden corpus's rule U (US only) is a note.
- **The "> 8 hotels" / "10 hotels" roll-out threshold** in TERMS and YC-L disagree; the entry does not use it.
- **Job titles.** Neither the agent nor the director is named in public; both are my choices (items 1 and 3).
- **The 5% is the founders' claim** for "the best" offices; no independent figure was sought.
- **UPFRONT_THEN has no "credited" or "money-back" flag**; the fee is a plain up-front amount (header).

screens.why_b4: Nothing on the page says what four holding beliefs mean for Codyco or what to do next, such as moving on to whether directors will pay €3,000 for the pilot; the only text under the verdict is my own problem statement repeated back.
screens.why_b5: The page never says that 7 people is a small sample, and it puts 'Holding up' directly over my 5%-missed and seven-figure claim, although nothing here measured a miss rate; Prevalence only shows that booking calls came in.
screens.instead: Say: 'All four problem beliefs held among 7 reservation agents, a small sample. This doesn't test the 5% miss rate. Next, check whether revenue directors will pay for the pilot.'

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up' sits right beside its deciding number, '7 of 7 said yes · bar 6 of 7', so I know the answer and why at once.
screens.why_b2: Seven cells all for me on a 0 to 7 axis with my bar marked at 6 (at least 8 in 10) reads at a glance: what is counted, over how many, and where the bar is.
screens.why_b3: My belief was that booking calls go unanswered, not that 'a booking call came in on their shift', which is just the circumstance every reservation agent is in; the condition that made it my problem is gone, so this is not my belief.
screens.why_b4: 'Common among these 7. How often, and whether it matters, are the next two cards.' points me onward but says nothing concrete about what this means for missed calls or for Codyco.
screens.why_b5: The gate asked whether any call came in, which every agent on any shift says Yes to, so 'Holding up 7 of 7' tells me my belief held when the missed-call problem was never tested and No had nobody to come from; the data cannot carry that claim.
screens.instead: Ask and show 'In the last 7 days, did a booking call on your shift go unanswered?', and count the agents who say No against me, so 'at least 8 in 10' can actually be refuted.

screens.why_b1: Holding up sits right beside 6 of 7 inside what I said against a bar of 5 of 7, with the median of 6 days, so I know both the verdict and the number that decides it.
screens.why_b2: The count of days, the 7 people and the bar at 5 are readable, but the tick row starts at 0 when nobody could answer 0, and the legend 'what you said · at what you said · short of it' took me a second look to match to the cells.
screens.why_b3: My problem is booking calls that go unanswered, yet the card's belief and question ask only whether a booking call came in on the shift, which is every shift at a hotel; the trailing '— the most recent time it happened' does not fit a count over 7 days either.
screens.why_b4: 'Whether it matters is the next card' points me onward but tells me nothing about what 6 of 7 means for Codyco, and it cannot, because calls arriving daily says nothing about how often one is missed.
screens.why_b5: n is visible and the small group is flagged as 'a lean, not a call', but 'Holding up' on the problem stage reads as if my missed-call frequency was confirmed when only incoming calls were counted.
screens.instead: Ask on how many of the last 7 days a booking call rang out unanswered on your shift, and tell me whether missing a caller is a daily event or a weekend one.

screens.why_b1: Holding up sits right beside 6 of 7 put it in their two and bar 5 of 7, so I can see the belief held and by how much, though the 6 of 7 line is printed twice in the verdict.
screens.why_b2: The caption says 7 people each picked two, 14 picks in all, and my row's 6 stands clearly above the rivals' 2s; the strip shows 6 for, 1 against and the marker at 5, so what is counted, over whom and where the bar sits are plain at once.
screens.why_b3: Importance and the line about five things being hard when booking calls go unanswered, with turning every caller into a booking in the top two, is word for word the belief I checked.
screens.why_b4: The So line properly warns that top two is not first place, but it never says what that means for Codyco, for example that Chiara's group, whose call center covers after hours, is the kind of buyer where this pain is weaker.
screens.why_b5: n=7 is visible throughout, 'a small group: a lean, not a call' says plainly that n is low, and the top-two-not-first caveat keeps the result from being read as more than it is.
screens.instead: 6 of 7 agents put answering every booking call in their top two. The one who didn't works where a call center already covers after hours, so lead with groups that have no night cover. 7 people is a lean, not proof.

screens.why_b1: The status 'Holding up' sits right beside its deciding number, 6 of 7 said today's way falls short against a bar of 5 of 7, and the strip and the chart (0+1+2+3+1 = 7) agree with it.
screens.why_b2: Each of my five rungs carries its count, the 'your line' marker shows where falling short begins, and the strip shows 6 for, 1 against, with the bar marker at 5 of 7, so what is counted, over whom and where the bar sits are plain at once.
screens.why_b3: The card is called Current solution, and its belief line and bar rung ('A few rang out, all called back that day') are word for word the ones I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: 'Your solution is judged against this gap on the next study' is close to generic: it does not tell me that 4 of 7 sit in the two worst rungs, where calls go unreturned or are lost, which is exactly the after-hours and peak gap my forwarding-to-AI idea should be pitched at.
screens.why_b5: n = 7 stays visible, the count line says 'a small group: a lean, not a call', and nothing claims more than these seven agents said.
screens.instead: Today's way falls short for 6 of these 7, and for 4 the calls that rang out were mostly or entirely lost; test on the next study whether answering those missed calls is what they would pay for, and remember this is seven people, a lean.

screens.why_b1: The status word 'Holding up' sits right beside '6 of 7 put it in their two · bar 5 of 7', and the line 'Importance held, 6 of 7; the 1 who said no' ties the verdict to the number.
screens.why_b3: The dimension is named Importance and the belief line is word for word the one I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: Nothing on the screen says what Chiara's answer means for Codyco; it does not say that groups whose call center already covers after hours may feel less of the missed-call pain, or that I should qualify for that before pitching.
screens.why_b5: The counts stay plain (1 against, 1 asked), but the Current solution card had 1 against and gets no box and no note under the boxes, while Prevalence and Frequency each get one, so I could wrongly read Importance as the only line with dissent.
screens.why_b6: Chiara's quote adds something I did not type: a call center after six already covers the hours I sell into, and group emails with no rates and rate parity across channels are what compete with missed calls for her attention.

screens.why1: As the first screen it is obvious why they ask whether I work in a hotel group's central reservations office before anything else.
screens.why2: Central reservations office and call center are the words we use for our own office, and the question reads in one go.
screens.why3: I take booking calls in our Munich central reservations office every shift, so I know the answer straight away.
screens.why4: Yes or no is complete for a gate, and a gate needs no escape.
screens.why5: It asks exactly the founder's segment, a central reservations office or call center of a hotel group in Germany, and nothing about any product reaches me.
screens.why6: It is one short question under 20 words, and yes or no is easy to hold when heard.

screens.why1: A recent-time question fits right after the screener, but asking whether a booking call came in on my shift on a trade-fair week in Munich is something I'd answer before you finished the sentence, so it feels like a wasted step rather than the real question.
screens.why2: Booking call and shift are my everyday words, and I understand it on first hearing.
screens.why3: I know exactly whether calls came in on my shifts this week, because they come in every hour.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it, and the chips belong to the story box after a Yes rather than the gate.
screens.why5: The problem was calls that came in and did not get answered, and this asks only whether a call came in, so it has lost the part that made it a problem.
screens.why6: It is short, one question, and ends in 'Yes or no', which I can answer at once.
screens.why7: The gate asks about the circumstance every reservation agent is in (calls come in on every shift), so everyone says Yes, No has nobody, and the founder's share can never be refuted.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, did a booking call come in on your shift that nobody answered? Yes · No

screens.why1: After I said yes to a booking call on my shift, asking on how many days one came in is plausible, but in our central office calls come in on every shift I work, so it reads as counting my shifts rather than getting at any problem.
screens.why2: Booking call, shift and days are exactly how we talk at the reservations desk, and I get it on first reading.
screens.why3: I know which days I worked last week and that calls came in on each of them, so I can answer from my own week.
screens.why4: One button per day from 1 to 7 with I can't recall set apart is complete and distinct, and my true answer, the number of shifts I worked, is there.
screens.why5: Nothing of the product leaks to me, but the founder's point was that not every call gets answered, and this asks only whether calls came in, so the meaning has drifted from the problem to the normal flow of work.
screens.why6: Short, one question, 'Say a number from 1 to 7' is easy to hold, and the escape is said once at the end.
screens.why7: The measure, shape and escape all meet the card: days of the window, 1 to 7, and I can't recall apart. But a call coming in happens on every shift worked, so my count tracks my rota rather than the problem, and the belief can hardly be refuted by what the buttons measure.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, on how many days did a booking call go unanswered on your shift? 1 · 2 · 3 · 4 · 5 · 6 · 7 · I can't recall

screens.why1: After asking whether booking calls came in on my shift and on how many days, asking which part of the shift I'd most like made easier follows naturally.
screens.why2: Rates on every channel, group requests and check-in rush are all words from my own trade, so I can answer on first reading.
screens.why3: I sit in a central reservations office in Munich, so the check-in and check-out rush and guests' requests at the desk are the front desk's work, not mine; I would only be guessing at those two.
screens.why4: Two rows belong to the front desk rather than a central office, two rows bundle two things, and my real trouble on a trade-fair Saturday (calls ringing out before I can pick them up) is only loosely covered by 'turning every caller into a booking'.
screens.why5: The founder's problem is booking calls that don't get answered at peak, after hours and on holidays, but the own row restates the whole job ('turn every guest who calls into a booking') rather than the calls going unanswered, so it drifted.
screens.why6: Five options said as a list is holdable, but 'getting through the check-in and check-out rush' and 'answering booking emails and group requests' are each two things in one breath and a mouthful heard once.
screens.why7: The own item is there and never first, and None of these is at the first ask, but the own row is swollen into the whole job and two rivals are another setting's work (front desk for a central office), so a central-office agent's picks are pushed toward the own row and the rules on rivals are bent.
screens.instead: Think of your last shift in the reservations office. Which one of these would you most like made easier? Answering every booking call before it rings out; keeping rates right on every channel; answering booking emails; handling group requests; or changing and cancelling existing bookings. Or say none of these.

screens.why1: After asking which part of the shift I'd most like made easier, asking how the calls actually went is the obvious next question.
screens.why2: The words are mine (rang out, called back), but 'how did answering a guest's booking call go' after 'your last booking call' is clumsy and needs a second read.
screens.why3: I know how my shift went with missed calls from the ACD board, but one booking call either got answered or it didn't, so I would have to guess what 'a few rang out' means for a single call.
screens.why4: The options describe a whole shift of calls, not the one call the stem asks about, and 'some rang out, called back when there was time' blurs into 'many rang out, few were called back'; in Germany a lot of missed callers also withhold their number, so 'couldn't call back' sits between them.
screens.why5: Nothing of a product or plan comes through; it is just how calls get answered and lost, in plain reservations-office words.
screens.why6: Five short options I can hold, but the stem repeats 'booking call' twice in one breath and the comma-split options are a bit of a mouthful heard at speed.
screens.why7: One measure (calls lost), five rungs best to worst, a working first rung, the last outright failure and the one escape are all in place, but the stem's occasion (one call) does not match options that measure a shift, which is the card's stem-versus-options pitfall.
screens.instead: Think of your last shift in the reservations office. How did the booking calls go? Every call answered or called back in minutes; a few rang out, all called back that day; some rang out, only some called back; many rang out, few called back; calls that rang out were simply lost; or say someone else took the calls.
